errors.current: After a preposition (here لِـ, 'to') and after a verb, -ūna becomes -īna.
errors.problem: The rule 'after a verb the ending is -īna / -ayni' is wrong as stated: a sound plural or dual that follows the verb as its SUBJECT keeps -ūna / -āni (the course itself has يَأْكُلُ الْمِصْرِيُّونَ in day 15 and يَأْكُلَانِ in day 20). Only the OBJECT of a verb (and a noun after a preposition) takes -īna / -ayni. A learner following the rule as written would produce *يَعْمَلُ الْمُوَظَّفِينَ. The same wording is repeated in the day-20 intro ('After a verb or a preposition the ending is ـَيْنِ') and in the dictionary tap glosses for ـِينَ ('masculine sound plural after a verb or preposition') and ـَيْنِ ('dual ending after a verb or preposition').
errors.fix: After a preposition (here لِـ, 'to') and as the object of a verb, -ūna becomes -īna.
errors.alsoChange: day20 intro: 'After a verb or a preposition the ending is ـَيْنِ' → 'As the object of a verb or after a preposition the ending is ـَيْنِ'; tap gloss ـِينَ → '-īna (ending: masculine sound plural as object or after a preposition; verb ending for you, to a woman)'; tap gloss ـَيْنِ → '-ayni (dual ending as object or after a preposition)'

errors.problem: The Arabic is correct, but the engine transliterates a final unmarked ي after ā as a long vowel: الشَّاي → 'sh-shāī' / 'ash-shāī' instead of 'sh-shāy'. Where the word is written with sukūn (شَايْ, days 15–16) the engine gives the right 'shāy'. Systematic: an unmarked ي after a long ā should be read as the consonant y.
errors.fix: Engine: treat an unvowelled ي after ā (and و after ā, e.g. in diptych words) as a consonant → sh-shāy; or vocalise the content consistently as الشَّايْ.
errors.alsoChange: transliterations ⟶ of all four lines follow automatically

errors.problem: When وَ or لِ is prefixed to a proper name the engine puts the capital letter on the prefix and lowercases the name, with no hyphen (Wadānyāl, Walaylā, Lidānyāl, Liyūsuf, Lisāmī), even mid-sentence. The Arabic is correct; the house style elsewhere is 'wa-Amrīkā', 'Wa-anā'. Expected: wa-Dānyāl, wa-Laylā, li-Dānyāl, li-Yūsuf, li-Sāmī.
errors.fix: Engine: when a one-letter prefix (وَ، فَ، لِ، بِ) precedes a token tagged 'name', output prefix + hyphen + capitalised name (wa-Dānyāl, li-Sāmī).

notes.note: 'آ (a + hamza) at the start means I' — the order is misleading; آ is hamza + long ā (as the tap gloss correctly says). Suggest 'آ (hamza + long ā)'.
مَقْهىً places the fathatān after the alif maqṣūra; the more usual print form is مَقْهًى (tanwīn on the hāʾ). Both are seen and the transliteration 'maqhan' is right; purely orthographic.
The name عَلِي is written without the shadda (strictly عَلِيّ, ʿAlī). It is consistent throughout and the engine still gives ʿAlī, so not counted as an error.

Transliteration hyphenation is inconsistent: wa-, bi-, li- are hyphenated before hamza/al- (wa-anta, bi-l-ḥāfila, li-l-ʿamal) but fused before a consonant (Wamādhā, wahiya, bisurʿa, liʾarbaʿa, wayadrusu). Style only, but a learner may not recognise وَ in 'Wamādhā'.
Dictionary glosses 'أَقْلَام=pen (plural)' and 'بُيُوت=house, home (plural)' read oddly next to 'كُتُب=books'; suggest 'pens' and 'houses'.

Final short vowels / tanwīn are dropped on nouns mid-sentence (مَكْتَب كَبِير, قَرِيب مِنَ النِّيل, عَصِير لَيْمُون) while the object -an is shown from day 15 on. This is a consistent course choice, not an error, but the owner may want to decide whether 'careful Arabic' endings should also appear in the week-2 sentences.
الْعَفْوْ is written with a sukūn on the final و (pausal form), like شَايْ and حُلْوْ elsewhere; consistent with the course's pausal spelling, fine.
مَسَاءُ الْخَيْر rendered 'Good afternoon' fits the story (hot afternoon) and is acceptable; the segs gloss 'evening, afternoon (of)' covers it.

summary: Read the whole export for days 11–20 (2,866 lines): every Arabic string with its harakat, the English and literal translations, all seg and tap glosses, all quiz answer keys and the mistakes right/wrong pairs, plus the generated transliteration. The Arabic itself is in very good shape: verb conjugations (singular, plural, dual, feminine -īna), colour agreement (aḥmar/ḥamrāʾ), object -an including the tāʾ marbūṭa case, number–noun gender polarity (عَشْر كَلِمَات vs عَشَرَة أَرْغِفَة, سَبْعَ مَلَاعِق vs سَبْعَة صُحُون), broken plurals with feminine-singular agreement, dual -āni/-ayni and هِيَ for non-human plurals are all correct, and every quiz answer key checked out. I found 4 errors: 1 major grammar-fact (the repeated rule that -īna / -ayni appear 'after a verb', which is wrong for a verb's subject and is contradicted by the course's own VSO sentences; should be 'as the object of a verb'), 1 minor gloss (حَارّ glossed 'hot (weather)' in the spicy-food lesson quiz), and 2 minor engine issues (الشَّاي → 'shāī'; capitalised fused prefixes on names such as 'Wadānyāl', 'Lidānyāl'). Eight notes cover orthographic and style points (tanwīn placement on مَقْهىً, عَلِي without shadda, hyphenation inconsistency, clumsy plural glosses, pausal spellings).
